QF.id: IV Clearing Settlement and Risk Management_35

question.text: What is the significance of the conversion factor in physical delivery of bond futures?

answer.text: It adjusts the invoice price to make different deliverable bonds with varying coupons and maturities comparable to the futures notional bond
It converts the futures price from percentage terms to rupee terms
It adjusts for the credit risk of different government bonds
It converts between clean and dirty bond prices

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook, the conversion factor is the price per rupee principal of the deliverable security to yield 7% (the notional coupon). It standardises deliverable bonds with different coupons and maturities so that the invoice price - computed as futures settlement price x conversion factor + accrued interest - reflects equivalent economic value across the deliverable basket. The Trap: The conversion factor is not a unit/format conversion (percentage to rupees) and it does not adjust for credit risk - all deliverable G-Secs are sovereign. Clean vs dirty price is handled separately by the accrued interest component in the invoice formula. Note: Source pages 247 and 250 support the deliverable-bond basket, the disclosure of associated conversion factors, and the invoice-price formula. The cheapest-to-deliver concept (lowest market price / conversion factor) is a standard application of this formula.
